messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Error when excuting make bin/libstan.a
parts:
My guess, because of where the problem occurred:

src/stan/agrad/matrix.hpp

that it's a memory issue. Windows in particular can
have trouble here because their compiler chain is less
memory efficient for some reason.

How much memory do you have?

Also, is this the latest version of Stan (1.3.0)?
And which version of g++ are you using? Try:

$ g++ --version

We should figure out how to release binaries, because
once this file's compiled, the rest are easy. We're also
working on reducing memory requirements during compilation.
But no intermediate releases to try yet. We're also changing
a bunch of other things and still testing.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Error when excuting make bin/libstan.a
parts:
On our Windows test machine, we are running the g++ distributed by RTools: gcc version 4.6.3 20111208 (prerelease) (GCC)

I just verified that I could run make bin/libstan.a using g++ 4.6.3 and with the default optimization levels.

If you can't change your g++ version, something that might work is playing with the optimization levels. The make variable is O and Stan's default is 3. The other options are 0, 1, 2, and s.

To set it to 0, run:
make bin/libstan.a O=0

You may have to clean in between attempts and to do that, type:
make clean-all




Daniel

More powerful as in more than 4GB of memory?

Also, is it a 64-bit version of the operating system?
32-bit Windows programs typically have a fairly lower upper
bound on per-process memory (under 2GB if memory serves),
which isn't enough to compile Stan (at least until we
break our libs apart into smaller pieces).

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Error when excuting make bin/libstan.a
parts:
On 5/19/13 4:05 PM, Daniel Lee wrote:
...

> If you can't change your g++ version, something that might work is playing with the optimization levels. The make
> variable is O and Stan's default is 3. The other options are 0, 1, 2, and s.
>
> To set it to 0, run:
> make bin/libstan.a O=0

...

The downside to doing this is that it will create a MUCH
slower version of Stan (up to a factor of 10 or possibly
more). Try to compile at as high an optimization
level as you can.

- Bob
